opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the more I understand the problem, the more humble I get about where we are, and at the same time, the more excited I am about where it's going.

When we started Meshy, I thought of 3D generation mostly as a geometry problem: can you produce a shape that looks right? Early on, that alone felt like a big milestone. You type a prompt or upload an image, and a few minutes later you get a textured mesh. That was genuinely new, and a lot of people were amazed just to see it work at all.

But as we worked with real users, game developers, 3D printing hobbyists, people making assets for film or XR, I realized "looks right in a thumbnail" is a very low bar. A production-ready 3D asset has many layers. You need clean topology so artists can edit it. You need good UVs, physically based materials that behave correctly under different lighting, sensible polygon counts, and for characters, rigging and animation that don't fall apart when the model moves. Each of those is its own deep problem. So in a way, the problem space expanded faster than our progress, which is a funny feeling. You climb one hill and realize it's actually a foothill.

So how do I assess our progress? I'd say we've moved from "impressive demo" to "genuinely useful tool" for a meaningful set of use cases, especially prototyping, indie games, and printing, where speed matters a lot and you can tolerate some imperfection. Quality has improved a lot, both geometry and textures, and the workflow integration has improved too. But for the most demanding professional pipelines, we're not yet at the point where you can just drop the output in and ship it without touch-ups. Being honest about that gap is important, because it tells us what to work on.

My background is in computer graphics and physical simulation, and one lesson from that world is that the last 10% of quality often takes 90% of the effort. 3D is harder than images or video in some ways: there's less data, the representation is more structured, and the output has to be usable by downstream tools, not just viewed. So I don't think we'll get there purely by scaling one model. It takes data, model research, and a lot of careful engineering around the whole pipeline.

Overall, I'd say we're still early. That's not a pessimistic statement; it's actually why it's so fun to work on. The goal hasn't changed: make 3D creation accessible to everyone, so anyone with an idea can turn it into a 3D asset. What's changed is that I now have a much clearer, more detailed map of how far that road really goes.

r001.rationale: The response says the problem is broader and more demanding than initially understood, and expresses excitement about future progress. It does not clearly say that this deeper understanding reveals a higher ceiling for what can be achieved.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the more I understand the problem, the more I realize how early we still are. When we started Meshy, I thought the hard part was getting a model to produce something that looks like a 3D object. We solved that fairly quickly, and for a moment it felt like we were almost done. Then real users showed up, and they taught us that "looks like a 3D object" is maybe ten percent of what they actually need.

A game artist doesn't want a pretty mesh. They want clean topology, sensible UV layout, textures that hold up under different lighting, a model that can be rigged and animated without falling apart, and a polygon budget that fits their engine. Every one of those is its own research problem, and many of them are harder than the generation itself. So my assessment keeps shifting. Each time we clear a bar, the bar we didn't know existed comes into view.

I'd say we've made real progress on quality and speed. A year or two ago, generating a usable asset took many minutes and a lot of luck. Now it's closer to seconds, and the hit rate is much higher. We've also gotten much better at listening. Our roadmap today is driven far more by what artists complain about than by what we think is technically exciting, and I think that's a sign of maturity.

But I try to stay humble about it. The gap between "impressive demo" and "I ship this in my production pipeline without touching it" is still large. I think of it the way I thought about Taichi earlier in my career. The elegant core idea is necessary, but the real value comes from grinding through the thousand unglamorous details that make something actually usable. We're in that grinding phase now, and I'd rather be honest about that than pretend we've arrived.

r001.rationale: The response says each milestone reveals another previously unknown bar and stresses how much work remains. It does not clearly say that solving more of the problem reveals a higher ceiling for what is achievable than originally imagined.

astra-6.text:
I think the more we understand the problem, the more we realize how much there is still to solve. You can generate something that looks convincing in an image, but a 3D model has to work from every angle. And if someone wants to use it in a game or another production workflow, appearance is only part of the requirement. The geometry, the textures, and the ability to edit it all matter.

So I would assess Meshy’s progress in terms of how much useful work we’re helping people accomplish. Can someone get from an idea to an asset they can actually use with less effort? As our understanding expands, that bar gets higher. That makes me optimistic about the progress, while also more aware of the distance we still have to go.

r001.rationale: The response says deeper understanding reveals more problems to solve and raises the bar for useful work, but does not state that the achievable ceiling is higher than originally imagined.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the more we understand the problem, the more we realize how much there is left to do. You can generate a 3D model that looks impressive in a demo, but making it useful is a much higher bar. Does the geometry make sense? Are the textures consistent? Can someone actually take it into their workflow and use it?

So I would assess Meshy’s progress on both the quality of the generation and how much work we save the user. We’ve made progress, but as the models improve, we also become better at seeing their limitations. To me, that’s a healthy process. The goal is to give people something they can create with, and that keeps pushing us to solve the next layer of the problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate says deeper understanding reveals more work and limitations, but does not state that it reveals a higher ceiling for what is achievable than originally imagined.
